clue.text: Trader's offer and female's dismissive reply?

parts.note: BOGOF is a shop's 'buy one, get one free' deal
F is the standard abbreviation for female; the 's joins it to the definition

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper pitches a bargain and a woman curtly tells them where to go.
explanation.walkthrough: BOGOF is British retail shorthand for 'buy one, get one free'; 'bog off' is mild British slang for 'go away'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rude British slang brush-off telling someone to go away, the sort of thing said dismissively.

clue.text: Bishop having sex atop church? Complain!

indicators.note: in a down clue the sex piece sits on top of the church piece, so it comes before it

parts.note: B is the chess notation for bishop
IT is a coy old word for sex appeal or sex itself

explanation.surface: A scandalous bishop up to no good above the church, and someone told to protest.
explanation.definitionFit: To bitch is informal for to grumble or moan about something, a slang synonym.

clue.text: Prime Minister who used to be happy with weight?

definitions.text: Prime Minister who used to be

parts.note: glad is a synonym of happy
a stone is a British unit of weight, fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: A question about a former premier who was once cheerful and heavy.
explanation.walkthrough: William Gladstone was a Victorian British Prime Minister, four times in office.
explanation.definitionFit: William Ewart Gladstone led four British governments in the nineteenth century, so a former premier.

clue.text: Nothing good comes on beginning to smoke them

definitions.text: Nothing good comes on beginning to smoke them

parts.note: FA, from 'sweet FA', is British slang for nothing at all

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word smoke is wanted

explanation.surface: A health warning: no good can come of starting to smoke cigarettes.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: 'them' are what you smoke, and the sentence says no good comes of starting. FAGS is British slang for cigarettes.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang cigarettes are called by this word, and the clue warns against starting on them.

clue.text: I back that woman to down one more stout

indicators.note: back asks for the word for 'I' to be written from end to start

parts.note: the self is the 'I', one's own person

indicators.note: to down is to swallow, so the woman's pronoun takes the numeral in

parts.note: her refers to that woman
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone backing a woman to sink another pint of stout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout' reads as the beer but is the adjective meaning fat; 'I' here is the self, read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Stout as an adjective means plump or heavily built, so its comparative matches having more flesh.

clue.text: Merciful nurse in story not without a heart

indicators.note: the nurse is placed inside the word for story

parts.note: a lie is a story, a made-up tale
EN is an enrolled nurse

indicators.note: the word not loses its middle letter, leaving its outside pair

explanation.surface: A kindly nurse appears in a tale that is not heartless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not without a heart' is the word NOT itself with its middle letter dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Being merciful means being forgiving and gentle in punishment, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Tourists express disappointment with Tango? Wise men

parts.note: to sigh is to show disappointment with a breath
T is Tango in the NATO phonetic alphabet
seers are prophets or sages

explanation.surface: Holidaymakers sighing over a tango lesson, alongside some wise men.
explanation.definitionFit: Tourists are visitors going round looking at a place's attractions, the very sense here.

clue.text: Opening time halves popular with retired men

indicators.note: the time letter splits the popular-plus-men string into two halves by sitting in its middle

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the soldiers' letters are read backwards

parts.note: OR, other ranks, means enlisted men

explanation.surface: Pub opening time cuts the evening in half for old soldiers in favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns OR into RO; T 'halves' INRO by sitting in its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: An intro is the introductory opening part of a piece of music or a talk.

clue.text: Learn Eve's about to get folk back into bondage?

indicators.note: about means scattered around, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A worry that learning about Eve leads back to servitude.
explanation.definitionFit: To enslave again is to return people to slavery, which bondage describes.

clue.text: Hope: a church's loftiest attribute?

parts.note: the spire is the tallest part of a church building

explanation.surface: A musing on hope as the highest feature of a church.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspire is to hope or strive for something, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Heard rank wind that'll make your eyes water

indicators.note: heard means the word for rank is taken as it is said rather than spelt

parts.note: a tier is a rank or row
gas is wind in the stomach

explanation.surface: Someone noticed a foul stench of wind strong enough to make you cry.
explanation.walkthrough: TIER said out loud sounds like TEAR, as in a teardrop.
explanation.definitionFit: Tear gas is a chemical irritant that causes the eyes to stream, used for crowd control.

clue.text: I'm turning in topless lace item worn by some retired

parts.note: 'Night!' is what someone says when going to bed

indicators.note: topless means the first letter of the word for lace is removed

parts.note: to lace is to tie, as with shoelaces

explanation.surface: Someone retiring for the night in a racy lace garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning in' means going to bed, and 'retired' means gone to bed, not stopped work. TIE topless is IE.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightdress is the garment worn in bed by those who have gone to sleep.

clue.text: Shut up hard American leader for hatefulness

parts.note: H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

indicators.note: the leading letter of hatefulness is taken

explanation.surface: A demand for silence from an American leader full of hate.
explanation.definitionFit: As a command, both mean be quiet and stop talking.

clue.text: Loose Independent clue is not to be beaten

indicators.note: beaten means battered into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A boast that an Independent crossword clue cannot be bettered.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose in the old moral sense means promiscuous or immoral, a synonym.

clue.text: Train held up around noon in remote areas

definitions.note: a plural phrase standing for a singular collective noun covering outlying regions

indicators.note: the rearranged letters wrap around the letter for noon
up means in disorder, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A train delayed around midday somewhere in the back of beyond.
explanation.definitionFit: The hinterland is the remote country lying far behind a coast or city.

clue.text: Chucked me pint on Republican (well-known)

indicators.note: chucked means thrown about, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A drinker complains that a pint was thrown at them by a famous Republican.
explanation.definitionFit: Prominent means important and widely recognised, a synonym for famous.

clue.text: Very drunk, but training to drink final Barolo?

indicators.note: the training letters swallow the word for final

parts.note: PE, physical education, is training
last means final
Barolo is an Italian red wine

explanation.surface: Legless after a training session that ended with Barolo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'final' is not a last-letter signal here; it is a plain synonym. Barolo stands for its colour, red wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Plastered is British slang for heavily intoxicated, a synonym.

clue.text: Old flame rejected cunning chap with tiny part?

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the word for cunning reads backwards

parts.note: art means cunning or craftiness

explanation.surface: A former lover spurned a sly fellow with a small part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns ART into TRA. The surface leers at 'tiny part'; it is a minor film role.
explanation.definitionFit: A walk-on actor in a film has a minor non-speaking role, hence a small part.

clue.text: Argentine bananas or another sort of fruit

indicators.note: bananas means crazy, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Argentine bananas, or some other kind of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' looks like the fruit but is the anagram signal; the fruit is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangerine is a small citrus fruit like a mandarin, a kind other than bananas.

clue.text: Turn away if vicar gyrates in centre of Bath

indicators.note: the turned vicar goes inside the central letters
the middle two letters of Bath are taken
gyrates means spins round, so the vicar's abbreviation turns back to front

parts.note: Rev, short for Reverend, is a vicar

explanation.surface: Look away if a vicar starts dancing in the middle of Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is an English spa city; here only its central letters are used.
explanation.definitionFit: To avert one's eyes is to turn them aside, a synonym.

clue.text: Clergyman scratching bottom before church worship

indicators.note: before puts the shortened clergyman word in front of the church letters
scratching means deleting, so the last letter of the clergyman word goes

parts.note: a reverend is a member of the clergy
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A cleric scratches his backside before going into church to pray.
explanation.walkthrough: REVEREND loses its final D to give REVEREN.
explanation.definitionFit: Reverence is deep respect or veneration, close to worship as a noun.

clue.text: US farmer cutting ends off boughs above river

indicators.note: in a down clue the trimmed word sits above the river letter, coming before it
the first and last letters of the word for boughs are removed

parts.note: boughs are branches of trees

explanation.surface: An American farmer lopping branches over a river.
explanation.walkthrough: BRANCHES without its ends is RANCHE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rancher runs a large cattle farm in the American West, an example of a farmer there.

clue.text: Underwear on a large nun of a certain sort

parts.note: a vest is a British undershirt
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A nun wearing a large-size vest.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a vest is the sleeveless undershirt, not a waistcoat.
explanation.definitionFit: Vestal virgins were the priestesses of Vesta in ancient Rome, a sort of chaste religious woman.

clue.text: Break wind and assert flamboyant vulgarity

indicators.note: break means smash apart, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Breaking wind and insisting on it is flamboyantly vulgar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break wind' reads as one phrase, but 'Break' is the anagram signal on WIND and ASSERT.
explanation.definitionFit: Tawdriness is cheap showiness, gaudy and in poor taste, so showy vulgarity.

clue.text: Drink Hoskins must get out of chap bringing food?

indicators.note: the setter's letter has to leave the word for the server

parts.note: a waiter brings food to diners
Hoskins is the setter, who refers to themselves as I

explanation.surface: The setter must stop being a waiter and go for a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Water is the most basic drink, fit for every table.

clue.text: Her Maj turned on yours truly, pure and simple

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the turned royal letters follow the self pronoun

parts.note: yours truly is a jokey way of saying me

indicators.note: turned means flipped round, so the royal letters read backwards

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: The Queen rounds on the speaker, plainly and simply.
explanation.definitionFit: Mere as an adjective means nothing more than, as in a mere child, simply that.

clue.text: Apply to be specialist? No pressure!

indicators.note: P stands for pressure in physics, so it is taken away from the specialist word

parts.note: an expert is a specialist

explanation.surface: A relaxed invitation to apply to become an expert, no pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: To exert force is to apply it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Praise song that man delivered for audience

indicators.note: spoken for listeners, so the pronoun is taken by its sound

parts.note: him refers to that man

explanation.surface: A tribute song performed by a man for the crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A hymn is a religious song of praise to God.

clue.text: School again? Gag! Regularly delay going in!

indicators.note: the picked letters go inside the gag word

parts.note: to gag is to retch

indicators.note: every other letter of the word delay is taken

explanation.surface: A frustrated teacher retching at another delay to school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gag!' looks like a joke but is the verb meaning to heave.
explanation.definitionFit: To school someone is to teach them, so to school again is to instruct them once more.

clue.text: Whenever City put on a bit of talent, I'm close to rapture

indicators.note: put on means placed after, so the city letters follow the word a

parts.note: NY is New York City

indicators.note: only the first letter of talent is taken

parts.note: the apostrophe is dropped, leaving two letters

indicators.note: the final letter of rapture is wanted

explanation.surface: A football fan promising rapture whenever City field a talented player.
explanation.definitionFit: Anytime means at whatever moment, the same as whenever.

clue.text: Those mocking vacuous dame and Hell's Angels?

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word dame keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: Hell's Angels are motorcycle riders

explanation.surface: Bikers and an airhead woman jeering at people.
explanation.definitionFit: Deriders are people who ridicule or scoff at others.

clue.text: Insignificant type involved in Shaolin sects

indicators.note: the answer is wrapped up in the letters of the words Shaolin sects

explanation.surface: A lowly member of a Shaolin martial-arts sect.
explanation.definitionFit: Insect is used figuratively for a contemptible, insignificant person.
